description: Sample round of 20 varied photos from the 1595/2025 william journal across 3 alternative 2025-phone style framings (60 images total).

framings.name: Framing A · 2025 Phone Main Lens (24mm Deep Focus, Balanced HDR)
framings.instruction: Captured as a candid, unposed photograph on a 2025 flagship smartphone main wide camera (24mm equivalent, f/1.8, deep focus across the scene). True-to-life 2025 digital color science, crisp sensor detail, balanced natural dynamic range, and spontaneous handheld framing from a 5 ft 7 in eye level—as if someone simply raised today's phone to keep what caught their eye in 1595. Everything in front of the lens is strictly authentic 1595 England (weathered timber, lime-plaster, hand-woven wool and linen, period tools and vessels, natural daylight or tallow flame). No sepia, no antique tint, no film grain, no scratches or vignetting, no painting or illustration texture, no staged historical-reenactment look, no added signs or legible lettering, and nothing modern in the frame.

framings.name: Framing B · 2025 Phone 2x Portrait Lens (50mm Shallow Depth of Field)
framings.instruction: Captured on a 2025 smartphone 2x optical portrait/telephoto lens (48-50mm equivalent, f/1.4, shallow depth of field with natural optical bokeh). Tack-sharp focus on the primary subject with the background falling into a soft, natural optical blur. Clean 2025 digital color science, high micro-contrast on tactile 1595 materials (unvarnished oak grain, hand-forged iron, coarse wool, damp lime-plaster, mud, tallow wax), and candid eye-level composition (5 ft 7 in). No sepia, no vintage color grading, no fake film grain, no vignette, no painterly brushwork, no theatrical costume staginess, no added signs or legible lettering, and nothing modern in the frame.

framings.name: Framing C · 2025 ProRAW Sensor (True Available Light, Zero HDR Shadow-Lift)
framings.instruction: Captured as an ungraded 2025 ProRAW digital photograph using only honest 1595 available light, with zero computational HDR shadow-lifting or stylized color grading. In low light, candlelight, or dusk, shadows fall into deep natural darkness and flames hold warm highlight roll-off without night-mode brightening; in daylight, contrast is crisp and unvarnished. Gritty, lived-in 1595 documentary realism—mud, coal soot, worn working cloth, damp stone, and uneven hand-built surfaces, caught mid-moment from a 5 ft 7 in eye level with nobody posing. No sepia, no antique filter, no film grain, no vignette, no painting style, no added signs or legible lettering, and nothing modern in the frame.

shots.title: The desk at first light
shots.photo_text: The desk at first light: the account book open at a fresh leaf, one line entered, quill, inkhorn, pounce-box and penny almanac, frost ferns on the pane. You are not in the picture.
shots.world_text: § 7.7 #1: The desk at first light: the account book open at a fresh leaf, one line entered, quill, inkhorn, pounce-box and penny almanac, frost ferns on the pane.
shots.subject_prompt: Seen from a standing man's eye level (5 ft 7 in) looking down at a plain scarred oak writing-table under a diamond-leaded casement window in a Bishopsgate lodging chamber on 1 January 1595 at grey first light. On the oak board: a narrow stitched paper account-ledger open at a fresh cream laid-paper leaf with a single line of dark brown iron-gall secretary-hand ink at the head (illegible cursive script), a goose-quill pen laid beside a horn inkwell, a small turned wooden pounce-box, and a small stitched penny almanac. On the leaded glass window-pane behind the desk, delicate white ice-fern frost patterns catch the cold winter dawn light. Cold dawn window light only; no candle burning, no people, no reflection in the glass, no modern stationery.

shots.title: Frost on the close
shots.photo_text: From inside the dark of the house doorway, at the eye level of a man standing there, looking along Great St Helen's. Hard frost. Each cobble is rimmed white, and the kennel is frozen. A shallow puddle by the Crosby Place gate is frozen white and opaque. The church porch is on the left, the elms bare. Beyond the close the roof-line of Crosby Place is black, with hoarfrost on the oriel mullions and one window lit. Timber houses overhang on the right, shutters closed, one small flame in a bracket. No people. A cat's prints cross the frost. The moon is not in the frame. No shadow of the man in the doorway falls on the stones.
shots.world_text: § 8.6 Photo 4 (S006): A narrow London close in January 1595, at night, seen from inside the dark of a house doorway under a jettied upper storey, at a standing man's eye level, so that no shadow of the viewer falls into the frame. Hard frost: the cobbles and the central kennel glitter, each stone rimmed white.
shots.subject_prompt: A narrow London close (Great St Helen's) in January 1595 at night, seen from inside the dark of a house doorway under a jettied timber upper storey at standing eye level (5 ft 7 in), so that no shadow of the viewer falls into the frame. Hard white frost rims every cobblestone and freezes the central drainage kennel. In the foreground, a shallow cart-rut puddle is frozen white and opaque, holding a glint of moonlight but no reflection. On the left is the squat stone porch and twin gables of a medieval parish church with bare winter elms. Beyond the close, above lower roofs, rises the long dark roof-ridge and tall carved stone oriel of Crosby Place, hoarfrost on the mullions and a single warm candlelit window. Overhanging timber-framed houses on the right with closed wooden shutters and one small tallow flame guttering in an iron wall-bracket. No people. A cat's paw-prints cross the frost. The full moon is out of frame behind the viewer, lighting the house-fronts cold blue-silver. Moonlight and one small flame only; no snow falling, no modern paving, no streetlamps.

shots.title: Fifteen barges
shots.photo_text: From the slope of Tower Hill, late morning, between the backs of the crowd. Fifteen barges row up on the flood below the Tower, close together, streamers and painted banners over them, trumpeters in the bows. White gun-smoke hangs low on the grey water. Wherries sit in the wake. At the left edge, a big man in a russet cloak, his back to the hill, leaning toward the gentleman in the lead boat as that gentleman steps out. The man's face is not turned. No one looks toward the picture. Richard is the man in the russet cloak.
shots.world_text: § 8.6 Photo 6 (S011): The River Thames below the Tower of London on 1 February 1595, late morning, seen from the crowded slope of Tower Hill at a standing man's eye level, between the heads and shoulders of citizens seen from behind.
shots.subject_prompt: The River Thames below the Tower of London on 1 February 1595, late morning, seen from the crowded slope of Tower Hill at a standing man's eye level (5 ft 7 in), looking between the heads and shoulders of 1590s London citizens in wool cloaks, flat caps, and felted hats, all seen from behind. Fifteen decorated wooden ceremonial barges row up close together on the flood tide toward the Tower wharf stairs, carrying painted silk streamers and heraldic banners (no text), trumpeters in the bows, and young gentlemen of the Inns of Court in black gowns and white ruffs. White black-powder gun-smoke hangs low over the grey river water. Wooden wherries bob in their wake; low roofs of Southwark on the far bank under pale, cold February cloud-light. At the left edge of the frame, a broad-shouldered man in a russet wool cloak, his back to the viewer and face unseen, leans forward watching a gentleman step ashore from the lead boat. Nobody looks toward the lens; sixteenth-century materials only, no modern vessels, no bridges in frame, no lettering.

shots.title: The yard before
shots.photo_text: The Rose yard before *Long Meg*: penny-standers pressing toward the stage, the flag up, winter afternoon light on the thatch.
shots.world_text: § 7.7 #9 (S016): The Rose yard before Long Meg: penny-standers pressing toward the stage, the flag up, winter afternoon light on the thatch.
shots.subject_prompt: Inside the open-air polygonal yard of the Rose playhouse on Bankside, Southwark, on a cold February afternoon in 1595 before the performance begins, seen from a standing man's eye level (5 ft 7 in) in the yard near the stage-right post. Penny-standers in worn 1590s wool cloaks, Elizabethan flat caps, knitted Monmouth caps, wool jerkins, and white linen coifs press forward over damp trodden earth and straw toward the raised oak thrust stage, all seen from behind—nobody turns toward the camera or poses. Three tiers of timber-and-plaster galleries rise around the yard under a steep reed-thatched roof catching pale winter afternoon sunlight, with a playhouse flag flying from the turret above against a cold grey-blue sky. No signs, no placards, no words on the stage balcony, no modern clothing.

shots.title: The rotted mortise
shots.photo_text: Close and low: the rotted mortise of a damp, sponge-soft oak ground-post at the Theatre, where James Burbage's knife went in, wet Shoreditch grass.
shots.world_text: § 7.7 #12 (G013): Close and low: the rotted mortise of a damp, sponge-soft oak ground-post at the Theatre, where James Burbage's knife went in, wet Shoreditch grass.
shots.subject_prompt: Close, low-angle view looking down at the base of a heavy weathered oak ground-post and sill-beam at the outer timber wall of the Theatre playhouse in Shoreditch on a damp February morning in 1595. At the pegged mortise-and-tenon joint just above the wet mud and stone footing, the aged oak timber is dark, waterlogged, and sponge-soft with rot, showing a fresh raw slot in the punky brown wood fibers where a knife blade was just pushed in to test the rot and drawn back out. Coarse, rain-wet green winter grass and mud press against the base of the timber in cold overcast morning daylight. No people, no hands, no knife left in the wood, no text.

shots.title: Twenty pounds on the long table
shots.photo_text: Twenty pounds in gold and silver on James Burbage's long table, the allocation sheet and ledger beside it, seven men's hands at the edges.
shots.world_text: § 7.7 #17 (S027): Twenty pounds in gold and silver on James Burbage's long table, the allocation sheet and ledger beside it, seven men's hands at the edges.
shots.subject_prompt: Seen from standing eye level looking down at James Burbage's long oak table in Holywell, London, on a March morning in 1595. In the middle of the worn oak board lies twenty pounds in Tudor coin—a small heap of hammered Elizabethan gold angels and neat stacks of worn silver shillings and sixpences—beside a loose rag-paper allocation sheet with roman-numeral columns and an open narrow parchment-bound account ledger, with a horn inkwell and quill nearby. Resting around the edges of the table are seven men's bare hands and wool-and-linen doublet cuffs of the company sharers (one right forefinger near the lower edge stained with dark ink). Framed from chest height down onto the table so no faces or heads appear in the picture. Natural north window light across the coins and paper; illegible period secretary-hand script only.

shots.title: The climb
shots.photo_text: Chalk-and-clay ruts shining amber in low sun on the climb through Chiltern beechwoods toward High Wycombe; the hired bay's ears.
shots.world_text: § 7.7 #19 (S030a): Chalk-and-clay ruts shining amber in low sun on the climb through Chiltern beechwoods toward High Wycombe; the hired bay's ears.
shots.subject_prompt: First-person view from the saddle of a horse climbing the rutted chalk-and-clay road through the Chiltern beechwoods toward High Wycombe on 26 March 1595 in late afternoon. In the lower foreground, the dark brown-tipped ears and bay neck crest of a hired bay horse frame the road ahead—no rider's face, body, or shadow visible. Ahead, deep cart-wheel ruts cut into wet white chalk and yellow clay, filled with water that shines warm amber in the low late-March sun slanting between tall grey beech tree trunks and last autumn's copper leaf-litter. Bare early-spring branches overhead; no fences, no gravel grading, no modern road signs, no people.

shots.title: The new oak
shots.photo_text: Chapel Street: black 1594 stumps beside a new oak frame raised pale, fresh lime-plaster, three children half-turned toward the frame and busy, a child's arm pointing, not posed
shots.world_text: § 8.6 Photo 14 (S032): A street in an English market town in early April 1595, eleven months after a great fire, seen at the eye level of a man walking. On the right of the street is a gap of three house-plots: blackened stone footings, a brick chimney-stack standing alone and smoke-stained, charred beam-ends, and new nettles coming through the ash. In the middle plot a new house-frame has been raised, fresh green oak almost yellow, pegged and braced, roofless against a soft grey sky.
shots.subject_prompt: Chapel Street in Stratford-upon-Avon in early April 1595, eleven months after a town fire, seen at the eye level of a man walking (5 ft 7 in). On the right of the unpaved street is a gap of three house-plots: blackened stone footings, a smoke-stained brick chimney-stack standing alone, charred beam-ends, fresh lime-plaster, and young green nettles coming through the ash. In the middle plot a new house-frame has been raised of fresh green oak almost yellow, pegged and braced, roofless against a soft grey April sky, with a carpenter sitting astride the wall-plate driving a wooden peg. On the left are unburned timber-and-plaster houses with thatch. A few paces ahead, three children are half-turned toward the new oak frame, caught mid-movement with their faces turned toward the building work and away from the viewer: a girl of eleven in a russet wool gown and white coif pointing at the burned plots, a boy of ten in a wool jerkin with a thin wooden lath toy sword over his shoulder holding up a bent iron nail to the light, and a girl of ten with her arm flung out shouting toward the carpenter. At the right edge, a woman in a grey gown carrying a leather fire-bucket steps from a doorway; at the bottom edge, the viewer's own hand holds a small woven rush basket. Wet cart-ruts, pale April sun; no church anywhere in frame, no posing, no lettering.

shots.title: Her hand on the rind
shots.photo_text: Anne at a stall judging a cheese, her hand on the rind; his own hand on the basket handle in the foreground
shots.world_text: § 7.7 #26 (W028): Anne at a stall judging a cheese, her hand on the rind; his own hand on the basket handle in the foreground.
shots.subject_prompt: Market day at the High Cross in Stratford-upon-Avon on an April morning in 1595, seen from standing eye level (5 ft 7 in) right beside a wooden trestle cheese stall. A woman of thirty-nine (Anne) in a plain grey-brown wool gown, white linen apron, and white linen coif stands in three-quarter back profile, her face turned away toward the stall as she presses her bare right hand firmly onto the natural rind of a heavy round farmhouse cheese resting on coarse linen cloth beside wooden butter firkins. In the immediate lower foreground, the viewer's own hand grips the braided rush handle of a market basket. Timber-framed market-town gables and busy market-women in the background under crisp spring daylight; nobody looks at the camera, no labels or signs.

shots.title: Pink at the tip
shots.photo_text: Hewlands from the lane: pink-tipped apple buds framing the long thatched roof and the sheep-hurdles
shots.world_text: § 7.7 #28 (W029): Hewlands from the lane: pink-tipped apple buds framing the long thatched roof and the sheep-hurdles.
shots.subject_prompt: Seen from a muddy country lane at standing eye level (5 ft 7 in) in Shottery near Stratford-upon-Avon on an April afternoon in 1595. In the near foreground, gnarled orchard apple branches with tight pink-tipped spring blossom buds and young green leaves frame the view across a damp green meadow enclosed by woven cleft-hazel wattle sheep-hurdles. Beyond the hurdles stands Hewlands, a long, low timber-framed Warwickshire farmhouse with cream lime-plastered panels and a deep, mossy weathered straw-thatched roof under soft April afternoon sunlight. No people, no modern fences, no wires.

shots.title: Sheets like washing
shots.photo_text: Damp sheets of the Plutarch hung to dry like washing. A pressman's arm on the bar. Type in its case below. Daylight from the shop door. No face. No mirror.
shots.world_text: § 7.7 #35 (S046): The press-room: sheets of the Plutarch hung to dry like washing, a pressman's arm on the bar, type in its case.
shots.subject_prompt: Inside Richard Field's printing house in Blackfriars, London, on a May morning in 1595, seen from standing eye level (5 ft 7 in). Overhead across the low-beamed timber workroom, freshly printed damp folio sheets of rag paper hang in neat rows over wooden drying-poles like linen washing, the dense columns of printed type visible only as fine dark ink texture and too small to read. To one side, a pressman's rolled linen shirt-sleeve and ink-smudged forearm pull the wooden bar of a heavy oak common hand-press, framed so no face or head appears in the picture. Below in the foreground, a slanted wooden type-case divided into small compartments filled with dark lead printing type sits on a bench, lit by bright natural daylight slanting in from the open shop door. No faces, no mirrors, no modern machinery.

shots.title: Firkins, a measure, a constable
shots.photo_text: The morning after: butter firkins on a stall, a market measure, a mended shutter, a constable with a bill leaning by them. He is bored. The firkins are set out as on any Saturday. Nothing is broken. Nobody argues with him. No crowd.
shots.world_text: § 8.6 Photo 24 Frame 1 (S059b): Leadenhall market in London on a June morning in 1595, seen at a standing man's eye level from the edge of the market floor under the great stone arcade. Wooden butter firkins are set out on a trestle stall as on any Saturday, and a market-woman in a white apron stands behind them. Leaning by the stall is a constable with a brown bill (a long-shafted polearm), bored, looking elsewhere.
shots.subject_prompt: Leadenhall market in London on a Saturday morning in June 1595, seen at a standing man's eye level (5 ft 7 in) from the edge of the stone-paved market floor under the medieval stone arcade. Hooped wooden butter firkins and a turned wooden cylindrical market measure are set out neatly on a trestle stall as on any Saturday, with a freshly mended wooden shutter behind and a market-woman in a white linen apron and coif standing behind them, looking down at her board. Leaning idly against a stone pillar beside the stall is a parish constable in a plain wool jerkin holding a brown bill (a long wooden-shafted iron polearm), visibly bored and looking away down the arcade. A scatter of clean straw on the stones; a few citizens with rush baskets passing in the distance. Soft early summer sun slanting through the stone arches; nothing broken, no crowd, no violence, no signs or lettering.

shots.title: A thumb short of the notch
shots.photo_text: A penny loaf on Mistress Ansell's bread-board, a thumb short of the notch. She has left it there. The notch is the old one, cut in a good year. Morning light. No face.
shots.world_text: § 8.6 Photo 24 Frame 2 (S059b): Back at the lodging: a plain wooden bread-board on a kitchen table, with a penny loaf lying on it. Cut into the board's edge is an old knife-notch, and the loaf falls short of it by a full thumb's width. Morning window light. Nothing else.
shots.subject_prompt: Seen from standing eye level looking down at a plain, scrubbed wooden bread-board resting on an oak kitchen table in a London lodging on a June morning in 1595. A single round crusted wheaten penny loaf lies on the board with its left edge flush against the end of the board. Cut clearly into the worn front wooden edge of the bread-board is an old, darkened V-shaped knife-notch from a plentiful year, and the small dearth-year loaf falls visibly short of reaching that notch by a full thumb's width. Natural morning window light slanting across the flour-dusted crust and worn oak grain; nothing else on the table, no knife, no hands, no face.

shots.title: The dressed close
shots.photo_text: A narrow close, seen from just outside a doorway under a jettied storey, at a standing man's eye. Every doorway is dressed: green birch over the lintels, fennel and St John's wort, and on one step an earthenware pot of tall white lilies. Over the nearest door a small lamp in a bracket is still burning, the flame pale in the daylight. At the end of the close the church porch stands with nobody in it. A little ash has blown into the kennel. Sparrows in the birch. No people, and no shadow of the man in the doorway.
shots.world_text: § 8.6 Photo 26 (S065b): A narrow London close on Midsummer morning 1595, about an hour after sunrise, seen from just outside a house doorway under a jettied upper storey, at the eye level of a standing man. Every doorway along the row of timber-framed houses has been dressed in the night: green birch boughs tied over the lintels, bunches of fennel and yellow St John's wort, and on one step an earthenware pot of tall white lilies.
shots.subject_prompt: A narrow London close on Midsummer morning (24 June 1595) about an hour after sunrise, seen from just outside a house doorway under a jettied timber upper storey at standing eye level (5 ft 7 in), with no shadow of the viewer in the frame. Every doorway along the row of timber-framed houses has been dressed overnight for St John's Eve: fresh green birch boughs tied over the oak lintels, bunches of green fennel and yellow St John's wort, and on one stone doorstep an unglazed earthenware pot of tall white lilies. Over the nearest doorway a small iron oil lamp in a wrought-iron bracket is still burning, its tiny flame gone pale in the early daylight. At the end of the close stands the squat stone porch of a medieval parish church, its oak door shut and nobody on the step. Low warm sun from behind the viewer's right lights the upper plaster storeys while leaving the cobbles and central kennel in cool shadow where a little grey wood-ash has blown in; house sparrows perched in the birch boughs; no people, no lettering.

shots.title: Short in the ear
shots.photo_text: Thin barley, short in the ear, close up; reapers small beyond; a thunderhead building over Edge Hill to the north-west.
shots.world_text: § 7.7 #58 (W063): Thin barley, short in the ear, close up; reapers small beyond; a thunderhead building over Edge Hill to the north-west.
shots.subject_prompt: Seen from standing eye level (5 ft 7 in) beside the unpaved Banbury road in Oxfordshire on a sultry afternoon on 30 July 1595. In the immediate foreground, stalks of sparse, weather-stunted summer barley—thin-stemmed and short in the ear—stand close to the lens at the edge of an open unhedged strip-field. Farther out across the field, small distant figures of country reapers in unbleached linen shirts, russet breeches, and straw hats bend with hand-sickles, their backs turned. On the distant horizon to the north-west above the long wooded ridge of Edge Hill, a massive dark slate-blue cumulonimbus thunderhead builds into the humid afternoon sky. No wire fences, no telegraph poles, no modern roads or machinery.

shots.title: The bench in apple-shade
shots.photo_text: The same bench by day, in apple-shade: inkhorn, two quills, the foul sheets. The stone from the night is still on the corner. No one is in the frame.
shots.world_text: § 7.7 #65 (W068): The same bench by day, in apple-shade: inkhorn, two quills, the foul sheets.
shots.subject_prompt: Seen from standing eye level (5 ft 7 in) in the walled back orchard garden behind the Henley Street house in Stratford-upon-Avon on a bright August morning in 1595. A heavy, weathered oak plank bench sits in the dappled green shade of low-hanging apple boughs loaded with small green-and-russet apples, with a rough stone-and-brick garden wall behind. On the bench plank lie a sheaf of cream laid-paper foul sheets covered in tiny illegible secretary-hand ink lines and cross-outs, weighted down at the corner by a smooth grey river stone left from the night before. A dark cow-horn inkwell is wedged upright into a natural knot-hole in the bench plank, with two white goose-quill pens lying beside the knot-hole. Morning sunlight filters through the apple leaves onto the paper and long orchard grass; no people, no faces.

shots.title: The crown and the sleeve
shots.photo_text: Burbage's hands on the property crown. Edith pinning the king's sleeve at the elbow. He holds still for her. The boards under them are bare. No face turned toward the yard.
shots.world_text: § 7.7 #73 (S093): Burbage's hands holding the property crown, and Edith pinning the king's sleeve at the elbow while he holds still.
shots.subject_prompt: At the tiring-house doorway at the edge of the bare wooden stage of the Theatre in Shoreditch on a September morning in 1595, seen from standing eye level (5 ft 7 in) and framed closely from shoulder to hip so no face is turned toward the lens. A player (Richard Burbage) in a worn crimson-and-murrey brocade stage king's doublet stands still, his two bare hands holding a gilded brass-and-pasteboard property crown at waist level. Beside his arm, the company seamstress (Edith) in a dark wool bodice and linen apron leans in with only her hands and lower profile glimpsed from behind, deftly pinning the seam of the king's sleeve at the elbow with brass straight-pins. Scuffed, unvarnished wide oak stage boards below them in cool autumn morning daylight from the open yard; no faces looking out, no modern zippers or tools.

shots.title: Nutshells at the end
shots.photo_text: After: gatherers carrying the boxes to the tiring-house, a boy sweeping nutshells in the yard at dusk.
shots.world_text: § 7.7 #77 (W085): After: gatherers carrying the boxes to the tiring-house, a boy sweeping nutshells in the yard at dusk.
shots.subject_prompt: The open-air yard of the Theatre playhouse in Shoreditch at dusk on 2 October 1595, just after the afternoon's audience has gone, seen from standing eye level (5 ft 7 in). In the foreground, a twelve-year-old playhouse boy in a plain wool jerkin, linen shirt, and wool hose, seen in three-quarter back view with his face turned away, sweeps crushed hazelnut shells across the trodden earth of the yard with a birch-twig besom broom. Beyond him toward the wooden stage and open tiring-house door, two gatherers seen from behind carry the small wooden-and-earthenware admission money-boxes indoors. Empty three-tiered timber galleries rise around the quiet yard under a fading deep-blue October twilight sky. No faces turned toward the viewer, no artificial lights, no signs or placards.

shots.title: The board by candle
shots.photo_text: Soft food by candle: the pottage bowl, the apple split and steaming, Gib's tail across the corner of the frame. No face.
shots.world_text: § 7.7 #79 (G078): Soft food by candle: the pottage bowl, the apple split and steaming, Gib's tail across the corner of the frame.
shots.subject_prompt: Seen from seated eye level looking down at a scarred oak supper board in a London lodging on a dim October afternoon in 1595, lit by a single burning tallow candle in a plain brass candlestick. On the dark oak board sit a glazed earthenware bowl of thick warm oat-and-herb pottage with a horn spoon resting in it, and a baked russet apple split open in half on a wooden trencher with a delicate wisp of steam rising in the candlelight. Across the lower right corner of the table lies just the striped grey furry tail of Gib the house cat, whose body is out of frame. Warm, intimate candlelit glow and soft shadows on oak, earthenware, and pewter; no people, no faces.

shots.title: The search, and nothing glinting
shots.photo_text: The hall floor after the play, seen looking down. Rushes, sweet-flag, and sprigs of dried rosemary, trodden and scattered. A boy of twelve is on his knees, his back three-quarters turned, parting the rushes with one hand and holding a short candle low in the other. The light is a small warm pool. At the edge of the pool, a yeoman's scarlet hose and shoe. Beyond that, carved wainscot goes into the dark. Nothing glints. Nothing is lifted out of the rushes.
shots.world_text: § 8.6 Photo 48 Frame 2 (S115b): The floor of a great hall at Richmond Palace late at night after a court play, Christmas 1595, seen from a standing man's eye level looking down and a little ahead. The boards are thickly strewn with rushes, sweet-flag and sprigs of dried rosemary, trodden and scattered. A boy of twelve in a plain shirt and hose is on his knees in the rushes, back three-quarters to the viewer, parting them with one hand and holding a short candle low in the other.
shots.subject_prompt: The floor of a great hall at Richmond Palace late at night after a Christmas court play on 27 December 1595, seen from a standing man's eye level (5 ft 7 in) looking down and a little ahead. The wide oak floorboards are thickly strewn with trodden rushes, sweet-flag, and sprigs of dried rosemary. A boy of twelve in a plain off-white linen shirt and dark wool hose is on his knees in the rushes, his back turned three-quarters to the viewer so his face is hidden, parting the rushes with one hand and holding a short burning tallow candle low in the other. The candle makes a small warm pool of light on the rushes while the rest of the floor falls away into deep darkness. At the edge of the warm light-pool stands only the lower leg of a Yeoman of the Guard in scarlet wool hose and a black leather Tudor shoe; carved oak wainscot is dimly visible in the dark background. Nothing is found and nothing glints in the rushes: the search is the picture. Candlelight only, no lettering.
